name: Neal Avron
sources: Sound On Sound — Secrets Of The Mix Engineers: Neal Avron (https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/secrets-mix-engineers-neal-avron)
notes: The emo/pop-punk producer-mixer of the 2003–2008 wave: 80–175 straight with the backbeat on 2&4 and the singles clustering 117–151. Two documented process facts govern this model. First, the **tracking order is drums → rhythm guitar → bass**, reversing the usual, because "when laying the rhythm guitars down first, it's much easier to tell whether the bass is out of tune" and it gives the bass "a place to fit" — so the bassline is `independent_riff` at 0.82 with root-and-octave motion, fitted around a guitar rather than locked to a kick. Second, compression is kept light — "**I use tape compression, and I don't want to flatten the transients**" — which is why the accent tier is wide and the velocity variance is real even though heavy pre-production fixes the parts before tracking and the grid stays hard. Three drum deltas are quoted: "kick 1 and the '&' of 3", "bright cracking snare on 2&4", and "16th tom fills into choruses", which is the tom-led perc block on a 4-bar schedule; the kit goes to a Studer A800 before Pro Tools, and the mic list is the reason the tone is described, not the pattern. Harmony is minor-leaning verses opening to major choruses with chromatic passing chords and a suspended pre-chorus, and his arrangements put the real hook in the pre-chorus. ⚠ `confidence` is medium because the research rates it high-medium and marks the harmonic claims **[LOW-CONF]** as inferred from the catalogue, which is why `keys` is left inherited. ⚠ Every drum probability here is **INFERRED**, as is `bpm.mode` 134.
